source_text: Would Labour win if young people voted? tl:dr: No, not on the popular vote anyway. I've often heard it said "*the Tories only win because old people vote*", I've probably said it myself at times. And while its definitely true that older people vote more than younger people I wondered if the difference was such that it actually changed the results so decided to check. Turnout figures for the last election looked like this, Age | Turnout :---|---: 18-24|43% 25-34|54% 35-44|64% 45-54|72% 55-64|77% 65+|78% *Source: Ipsos Mori, How Britain voted 2015* Turnout is strongly correlated with age, as is likelihood of voting Tory: Age|Con|Lab|LD|UKIP|Green|Oth ---|---:|----:|----:|----:|----:|----: 18-24|27%|43%|5%|8%|8%|9% 25-34|33%|36%|7%|10%|7%|7% 35-44|35%|35%|10%|10%|7%|6% 45-54|36%|33%|8%|14%|7%|5% 55-64|37%|31%|9%|14%|7%|7% 65+|47%|23%|8%|17%|7%|3% *Source: Ipsos Mori, How Britain voted 2015* Based on this information you can create a simple model for popular vote share by multiplying voting share at that age group by that age groups turnout and the number of people of that age (I used the 2011 census numbers). You can then play around with what the results would look like in different hypothetical turnout scenarios. I considered three situations: a) actual - as shown above; b) everyone votes - every eligible person at every age group votes; and c) everyone under 35 votes - The most optimistic scenario for Labour, every person under 35 votes and turnout at other ages remains as it actually was. The results are shown below, Party | Actual | Everyone votes | All u35 vote ---|---:|----:|----: Con|36.4%|35.7%|35.3% Lab|30.7%|31.8%|32.2% LD|7.9%|7.8%|7.6% UKIP|12.6%|12.2%|12.0% Green|6.9%|6.9%|7.0% Oth |5.4%|5.7%|5.9% So in short while the gap would close, even in the most optimistic scenario for Labour, the Tories would have still won the popular vote. The other surprising result from this was how little the green party benefit from increased young turnout, I expected them to show the biggest difference but it seems that their support is actually broadly even across the age range. Caveats: This is a very simple and rough model, it doesn't say anything about constituencies or seats. In actual fact the impact in a few key swing seats could have the power to change which party was actually elected. In addition it is based on post election surveying which will not exactly represent the actual results and the no. of voters is based on census information which will include people not eligible to vote. [Edit to add] Another issue is the implicit assumption that non voters would divide up between the parties in the same way that voters do. This would probably be fine to assume if 100% of non-voters didn't vote because they couldn't be bothered or didn't care. However presumably some proportion of non-voters are in that group because they don't feel that there is a party which represents their views. Depending on the relative size of this group that assumption would become less valid. The full calculations are shown here, http://imgur.com/FR2c0zm

source_text: [Debunk this]Carl Sagan settled an argument between Stanley Kubrick and Arthur C. Clarke about how aliens should look in their film 2001 Carl Sagan told a story in which he met with director Stanley Kubrick, who asked for his advice about the ETs in *2001: A Space Odyssey* - what they should look like. According to Sagan, Kubrick had been arguing about this with writer Arthur C. Clarke. Sagan claimed he suggested to Kubrick that the ETs not be shown in the film, which of course was the solution Kubrick used. This subreddit encourages contributers to debunk their own bunk, so I'll offer this. My thanks to a fellow subredditor - u/Tisias - who succeeded in getting this falsehood removed at least from the Front Page. At present, it's still at TIL. https://www.reddit.com/r/todayilearned/comments/4c3t9n/til_carl_sagan_was_brought_in_to_mediate_an/ "Anthony Frewin (longtime Kubrick's aide) settled the record straight, and talking about Sagan's story (that appeared also in the scientist's biography A life, pp.178-9), he says:" >[...] This makes a good story, but it is simply not true. SK was exploring ideas for the aliens later in 1965 and through 1966 when Christian Kubrick was still sketching designs and I continued researching Giacometti's sculptures (SK was much taken with them), Max Ernst paintings and fantastic art generally, looking for alien ideas. None of this would have been done had SK followed Sagan's advice. SK realized himself in the end that showing them was a Bad Idea, just as the end pie fight in 'Dr. Strangelove' was also a Bad Idea and was similarly abandoned. (Are we alone?, p.13) >In a interview given in the same year about the editing of the book The Stanley Kubrick Archives (where, for the first time, many images of the aliens were published) Frewin gives a slightly different account, adding some depth to the topic: The aliens were never going to be shown in the film. Stanley considered – but only considered – showing them. He was not happy with how they came out (remember, this was long before CGI) and that – coupled with his realization, from a dramatic point of view, that it was better not showing them – deep-sixed the idea. It appears that Carl Sagan, the great de-mystfier and debunking enthusiast, has been debunked.
